meta.what: Grammar rulings made by the project owner, one per open area of research/data/grammar-gaps.json. Each starts provisional and is frozen after one release in use.
meta.source: docs/decisions-log.md records each ruling with the owner's words and the evidence.

rules: One form serves as both subject and object for I, we, you, he, she and it.
Nust is 'they' and niin is 'them'.
Hi is 'you' for one person or many.
An object pronoun may be left out where the meaning is clear.
Reflexives use the plain pronoun. Nimaar is kept for 'itself' as emphasis.
Dovah for 'me' is a style for dragon speakers in role play. It is not the standard pronoun: a learner is a person, not a dragon.

forms.note: the one subject use is in a later game; said 'hee'

rulings.basis: The summary table of the Thuum.org Fifth Edition, tested against the game texts. Counts are tokens in the game texts with duplicate records left out.
rulings.carried_forward: Words for 'its' and 'their' are settled with possession (proposal 11). The owner proposed coining niist for 'their'.

rulings.area: G11 Questions: how a question is formed
rules: A question may be formed in any of the three ways the game shows. All three are correct.
1. A question word comes first: Wo meyz wah dii vul junaar? (Who comes to my dark kingdom?)
2. The verb moves in front of the subject: Boaan tiid ...? (Has the time come ...?), beside the statement Tiid boaan. (The time has come.)
3. A statement is said with a questioning tone: Ful, losei Dovahkiin? (So, you're the Dragonborn?)
rulings.basis: The five questions in the game's dragon-language text. Each of the three patterns is attested once.
rulings.carried_forward: Question words: wo who and wen whose are the game's. Waar what, wil where, wuz when, wul why and wed how were coined for this project and accepted by the owner on 2026-11-19; see forge-words.json. The game's fod and rul (when) and kolos (in which) remain joining words.
examples_with_the_new_words: Wul drey hi dreh daar? (Why did you do that?)
Wed drey rok dir? (How did he die?)

rulings.area: G07 Possession: the endings on the noun
rules: The endings are: -i my; -i'il your; -i'i his, her or its; -u our.
In -i'i and -i'il the two i's are separated by a glottal stop, as the two u's are in thu'um, and the standard spelling writes the apostrophe.
This applies only to these endings. Inside a word the doubled i is one long 'ee' and is unchanged (Dovahkiin, krii, tiid).
A noun that already ends in ii takes the stop and the rest of the ending: zii (soul), zii'il (your soul), zii'i (his soul).
Game texts are shown as the game wrote them (bormahii, zaamiil, ziil), and those spellings are accepted variants.
rulings.owner_words: we're going to treat the i'i like thu'um, like a glottal stop; then, asked how far it reaches: let's go with 1 (the endings only)
rulings.why: Under the reading convention i and ii are the same sound, so 'my' (-i) and 'his' (-ii) were written differently and said alike. The owner had called this systematically problematic.
rulings.note: The stop in these endings is this project's convention. The game writes them with the single double-i rune, and nothing is known of how its voice actors say them.
rulings.in_runes: As with u'u: two separate I runes, with the break mark between them once that sign is designed. The single double-i rune stands for the long vowel inside a word.

rulings.area: G07 Possession: the two ways, 'its', 'your', and 'of'
rules: Possession is shown in either of two ways, and both are standard: a separate word before the noun, or an ending on the noun. The checker accepts either.
The separate words are dii (my, mine), hin (your), ok (his), ek (her), un (our) and niist (their). Niist was coined for this project.
The endings are set out under G07-possessive-endings.
'Its' is the ending -i'i. There is no separate word for it.
Hin is the standard 'your'. Him occurs once in the game and is a rare variant.
For 'of' between two nouns, do is the general word. Se joins the parts of a compound.

examples.from: built from the rules, with a coined word

rulings.basis: Counts in game text: dii 9, hin 21, him 1, ok 25, ek 4, un 1; endings -i 20, -ii 15, -iil 1, -u 5; do 82. The official definition of se says it should be used when new words are formed.

rulings.area: G09 Tense and aspect, with G13 the copula
rules: A verb has one form. It does not change for person or number.
Marking time is optional. The plain verb can mean present, past or ongoing, and the checker never marks an unmarked verb wrong.
To mark the past: drey + verb. To mark the future: fen + verb. Fent + verb is the solemn 'shall'.
'Have done' may be said either way: lost + verb, or the verb with -aan. The -aan form also serves as the describing word ('fallen', 'killed').
A new -aan form is made by adding -aan. The game's irregular ones are kept as they are: kriaan from krii, mahlaan from mah, naako.
'To' before a verb is wah + verb.
Los is 'is' and 'are'; lost is 'was' and 'have'; kos is 'be', used after fen and fent. Los may be left out where the meaning is clear.
The ending -a or -ha for 'to' is not taught for new sentences. The two game words that carry it, vokriiha and funta, are recognised and explained.

examples.text: wen zii fen mahfaeraak aak ok brod
examples.meaning: whose spirit will forever guide his clan
he is the herald of glory

rulings.basis: Game text: fen 16 tokens, 15 directly before a verb; fent 4; drey 6; wah + verb 23. The perfect is made with -aan alone, with lost + verb, and once with both (lost kriaan). The -a or -ha ending rests on two tokens that do not show the same construction, and the four example forms in the Thuum.org summary do not occur in the game. The makers stated that tense is optional.
